questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
Tests understanding of namespace isolation and basic egress filtering using NetworkPolicy. It checks hands-on ability to craft minimal, enforceable rules and verify them.

## Key Concepts
- Kubernetes NetworkPolicy basics
- Namespace-scoped isolation
- Egress rules and default deny
- Basic verification via kubectl and logs

## Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: test-egress-isolate
  namespace: test
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes:
  - Egress
  egress:
  - to:
    - ipBlock:
        cidr: 10.1.2.3/32
    ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 443
  - to:
    - namespaceSelector: {}
      podSelector:
        matchLabels:
          app: dns
    ports:
    - protocol: UDP
      port: 53
  - to:
    - ipBlock:
        cidr: 0.0.0.0/0
        except:
        - 255.255.255.255/32
    ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 53
```

```yaml
# Compliant Pod in test namespace
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: compliant-pod
  namespace: test
spec:
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: busybox
    command: ["sh", "-c", "sleep 300"]
```

```yaml
# Noncompliant Pod in test namespace (tries to access prod)
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: noncompliant-pod
  namespace: test
spec:
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: busybox
    command: ["sh", "-c", "wget http://prod.svc.cluster.local || true"]
```

```yaml
# DNS test Pod (for compliance with DNS allow rule)
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: dns-test
  namespace: test
spec:
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: busybox
    command: ["sh", "-c", "nslookup kubernetes.default.svc.cluster.local"]
```

## Follow-up Steps
- kubectl apply -f policy.yaml
- kubectl apply -f compliant-pod.yaml; kubectl exec compliant-pod -- curl logs.internal:443
- kubectl apply -f noncompliant-pod.yaml; observe failure to reach prod
- Check events: kubectl describe networkpolicy/test-egress-isolate -n test

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
Tests ability to design a reject-by-default policy for hostPath usage, a common attack surface, and to describe how to maintain a dynamic allowlist in production.

## Key Concepts
- Gatekeeper ConstraintTemplate and Constraint
- hostPath volumes and host filesystem access risk
- dynamic allowlist via a ConfigMap and a small controller to sync data
- CI validation (dry-run, gatekeeper admissions) and runtime validation

## Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: templates.gatekeeper.sh/v1beta1
kind: ConstraintTemplate
metadata:
  name: HostPathPolicy
spec:
  crd:
    spec:
      names:
        kind: HostPathConstraint
  targets:
  - target: admission.k8s.gatekeeper.sh
    rego: |
      package hostpathpolicy
      violation[{"msg": msg}] {
        input.review.kind.kind == "Pod"
        some i in input.review.object.spec.volumes
        input.review.object.spec.volumes[i].hostPath
        not data.hostpath_allowlist.namespaces[_]
        msg := "hostPath volumes are forbidden unless in allowlist"
      }
```

```yaml
apiVersion: constraints.gatekeeper.sh/v1beta1
kind: HostPathConstraint
metadata:
  name: hostpath-deny
spec:
  match:
    kinds:
    - apiGroups: ["v1"]
      kinds: ["Pod"]
```

Compliant manifest (no hostPath):
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: compliant-pod
  namespace: default
spec:
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: nginx:1.23
```

Noncompliant manifest (hostPath present):
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: noncompliant-pod
  namespace: default
spec:
  volumes:
  - name: data
    hostPath:
      path: /var/lib/data
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: nginx:1.23
    volumeMounts:
    - mountPath: /data
      name: data
```

CI/runtime validation plan: run Gatekeeper admission checks on PRs, simulate allowed namespaces via the ConfigMap sync, and perform a runtime audit post-deploy using a test pod to verify policy enforcement.

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
Security hardening of Kubernetes manifests is a practical, repeatable gate in real projects. This tests understanding of policy-as-code, tooling choices (Kyverno vs Gatekeeper), constraint design for host access controls and image source controls, and CI integration in GitHub Actions with ephemeral test clusters.

## Key Concepts
- Policy-as-code with Kyverno or OPA Gatekeeper
- Constraints for host access (hostNetwork, hostPath, hostPort, privileged containers)
- Image source controls (allowed registries) and imagePullPolicy enforcement
- CI integration in GitHub Actions using KinD or similar ephemeral clusters

## Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: kyverno.io/v1
kind: ClusterPolicy
metadata:
  name: deny-host-access
spec:
  rules:
  - name: block-host-network
    match:
      resources:
        kinds:
        - Pod
    validate:
      message: "hostNetwork is not allowed"
      pattern:
        spec:
          hostNetwork: "false"
  - name: block-host-path
    match:
      resources:
        kinds:
        - Pod
    validate:
      message: "hostPath volumes are not allowed"
      deny:
        conditions:
        - key: "{{ contains(element.volumes[].hostPath, '') }}"
          operator: "NotEqual"
          value: ""
```

## Minimal Policy (Combined)
```yaml
apiVersion: kyverno.io/v1
kind: ClusterPolicy
metadata:
  name: security-guardrails
spec:
  rules:
  - name: deny-host-network-port
    match:
      resources:
        kinds:
        - Pod
    validate:
      message: "hostNetwork and hostPort are not permitted"
      pattern:
        spec:
          hostNetwork: "false"
          hostPort: "0"
  - name: deny-host-path
    match:
      resources:
        kinds:
        - Pod
    validate:
      message: "hostPath volumes are not permitted"
      deny:
        conditions:
        - key: "{{ @ }}"
          operator: "AnyNotIn"
          value: [""]
      foreach:
        - list: "spec.volumes[?hostPath]"
          deny: true
  - name: deny-privileged-containers
    match:
      resources:
        kinds:
        - Pod
    validate:
      message: "Privileged containers are not permitted"
      pattern:
        spec:
          containers:
          - securityContext:
              privileged: "false"
  - name: allowed-registries
    match:
      resources:
        kinds:
        - Pod
    validate:
      message: "Images must come from approved registries"
      pattern:
        spec:
          containers:
          - image: "registry.company.com/*"
            imagePullPolicy: "Always"
```

## Failing Manifest (hostPath + hostNetwork)
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: insecure-pod
spec:
  hostNetwork: true
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: docker.io/myapp:latest
    securityContext:
      privileged: true
    volumeMounts:
    - name: host-volume
      mountPath: /data
  volumes:
  - name: host-volume
    hostPath:
      path: /etc
```

## Passing Manifest
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: secure-pod
spec:
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: registry.company.com/myapp:v1.0
    imagePullPolicy: Always
```

## Local Validation
```bash
# Install Kyverno locally
brew install kyverno

# Apply policies
kubectl apply -f security-guardrails.yaml

# Validate a manifest
kyverno validate insecure-pod.yaml
```

## CI Validation (GitHub Actions)
```yaml
name: Validate Manifests
on: [pull_request]
jobs:
  validate:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
    - uses: actions/checkout@v4
    - name: Create KinD cluster
      run: kind create cluster
    - name: Install Kyverno
      run: |
        kubectl apply -f https://github.com/kyverno/kyverno/releases/latest/download/install.yaml
        kubectl wait --for=condition=ready pod -l app=kyverno -n kyverno --timeout=120s
    - name: Apply policies
      run: kubectl apply -f security-guardrails.yaml
    - name: Validate manifests
      run: |
        kubectl apply --dry-run=server -f insecure-pod.yaml || echo "Expected failure"
        kubectl apply --dry-run=server -f secure-pod.yaml
```

## Why This Is Asked
Tests ability to design multi-facet security gates across image provenance, container hardening, IAM, and network posture within a Helm-based workflow. It also assesses tooling integration (cosign, Kyverno, OPA) and practical verification.

## Key Concepts
- cosign image signing and repo-backed public keys
- Helm chart security: readOnlyRootFilesystem, runAsNonRoot
- RBAC least-privilege patterns in Kubernetes
- OPA/Kyverno policies for mTLS and egress controls

## Code Example
```yaml
# Kyverno policy snippet enforcing readOnlyRootFilesystem and runAsNonRoot
apiVersion: kyverno.io/v1
kind: ClusterPolicy
metadata:
  name: enforce-container-security
spec:
  validationFailureActions: enforce
  rules:
  - name: require-security-context
    match:
      resources:
        kinds: [ Deployment, DaemonSet, StatefulSet ]
    validate:
      message: "Containers must run as non-root and with readOnlyRootFilesystem"
      pattern:
        spec:
          template:
            spec:
              securityContext:
                runAsNonRoot: true
                readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
```

- How would you test the CI gate against a large repo with many charts? 
- What trade-offs exist between strict mTLS enforcement and operational flexibility?

## Why This Is Asked
This checks IaC policy thinking and beginner-friendly gate design for real-world Terraform repos.

## Key Concepts
- Terraform plan JSON, OPA/rego, policy-as-code, resource-type checks (snowflake_share, aws_s3_bucket).
- Handling create actions and how to surface violations in CI.

## Code Example
```rego
package terraform.enforcement

default allow = false

violation[{"msg": m}] {
  rc := input.resource_changes[_]
  rc.type == "snowflake_share"
  rc.change.actions contains "create"
  not rc.change.after.tags.approved == true
  m := "Snowflake share must have tags.approved=true"
}

violation[{"msg": m}] {
  rc := input.resource_changes[_]
  rc.type == "aws_s3_bucket"
  rc.change.actions contains "create"
  (not rc.change.after.server_side_encryption_configuration) or (rc.change.after.public_access_block != true)
  m := "S3 bucket must enable encryption and block public access"
}
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you adapt this for existing resources?
- How to extend to other providers/resources and monitor drift?

## Why This Is Asked

This question evaluates practical supply chain security controls in multi-cloud Kubernetes environments. It assesses familiarity with policy-as-code, container image signature verification, and SBOM (Software Bill of Materials) attestations integrated into CI/CD pipelines.

## Key Concepts

- **Image Provenance:** Cosign and Sigstore provide cryptographic verification that container images have not been tampered with and originate from trusted sources.
- **SBOM Attestations:** Software Bill of Materials documents enumerate software components, enabling vulnerability tracking and compliance verification.
- **Policy-as-Code:** Gatekeeper and Kyverno enforce admission control policies as code, ensuring consistent security enforcement across clusters.
- **Multi-Cloud Complexity:** Different cloud providers require unified security controls; policy engines provide a vendor-agnostic approach to image verification.

# Minimal Kyverno policy snippet (illustrative)
apiVersion: kyverno.io/v1
kind: ClusterPolicy
metadata:
  name: require-edge-attestation
spec:
  validationFailureAction: enforce
  background: true
  rules:
  - name: require-attested-node
    match:
      resources:
        kinds: [Deployment]

## Why This Is Asked
Dives into practical container security beyond basic signing, SBOM integration, and cross-cloud trust boundaries.

## Key Concepts
- Image signing with Cosign
- SBOM (CycloneDX) and attestations
- Kyverno/OPA for provenance policies
- Registry allowlists and digest pinning
- CI/CD integration and stage/production verification

## Code Example
```yaml
# Example Kyverno policy (illustrative)
apiVersion: kyverno.io/v1
kind: ClusterPolicy
metadata:
  name: image-provenance
spec:
  validationFailureAction: Fail
  rules:
  - name: require-cosign-signed
    match:
      resources:
        kinds: ['Deployment','DaemonSet','StatefulSet']
    verifyImages: true
  - name: require-sbom-annotation
    match:
      resources:
        kinds: ['Deployment','DaemonSet','StatefulSet']
    validate:
      message: 'SBOM annotation missing'
      pattern:
        metadata.annotations: {'io.github CycloneDX SBOM': '*'}
```
